# Throughline — This Week in AI · 2026-11-23

Since last week, Anthropic's IPO has closed and the new Congress is sharpening its AI agenda — two storylines this edition examines. Meanwhile, two quieter but consequential developments arrived: a Nature Machine Intelligence paper upending assumptions about how AI actually works inside, and hard payroll data confirming that AI is reshaping who gets hired before anyone gets fired.

## Anthropic's IPO Lands — and So Do the Doubts (developing)

Anthropic priced its IPO on November 19 at $83 per share, raising $81.3 billion — the largest public offering in history, surpassing SpaceX's June 2026 record of $75 billion [1][2]. The stock opened at $111.50 and closed its first day at $97.17, giving Anthropic roughly a $1.5 trillion fully diluted market cap [3][4]. The company generated $33.2 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026 but ran a $1.26 billion operating loss, and sequential revenue growth decelerated from 75% in Q2 to 48% in Q3 — a pattern Wall Street is watching [5][6]. Former SEC chair Gary Gensler warned publicly that an AI investment bubble could burst before the 2028 election, and the IPO day itself was shadowed by Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation from Nvidia [7][8]. For builders: the gap between Anthropic's market cap and its operating losses means pressure to convert Claude into revenue-generating enterprise products will intensify sharply.

## AI Is Not Hiring Juniors (new)

Employment for workers aged 22–25 in AI-exposed occupations now sits 19% below expected baseline trends — a gap that widened from 15% in mid-2025 — according to the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries Dashboard, built jointly with ADP Research on live payroll data [9]. The mechanism is reduced hiring, not layoffs: Goldman Sachs research corroborated that the anticipated "AI layoff wave" has not materialised, but positions are simply not being opened [10]. Coface's sector analysis and the Stanford/ADP payroll data converge on the same occupational pattern: administrative, accounting, information technology, and sales roles face the steepest exposure, with computer programmers at 75% AI task coverage among the most affected [11]. Workers who do hold AI skills command an average wage premium of 62% — up from 57% — peaking at 118% in consumer markets, according to PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer [12]. For practitioners building with AI: the talent bifurcation is already showing in payroll data, meaning teams that delay AI upskilling programmes are not just risking productivity — they are likely already paying a premium to recruit.

## AI and the Brain Are Not the Same Thing (new)

A York University team publishing in Nature Machine Intelligence (Muzellec & Kar, 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0) found that artificial neural networks and biological brains arrive at similar predictions of neural responses through fundamentally different internal mechanisms [13]. Using a new "reverse predictivity" test — checking whether brain activity can predict AI model features, not just the reverse — the researchers showed that while AI models predict primate brain activity reasonably well, the brain cannot predict the AI models' internal representations; the study also challenges the assumption that brain-inspired architectures mimic cognition, and the team released a toolkit for identifying which parts of AI networks genuinely correspond to biological activity [13]. The finding matters for AI interpretability research: if AI and brains use different internal strategies, neuroscience-derived intuitions about how to open the "black box" may be systematically misleading.

## Congress Sets Its AI Agenda — Against a White House Headwind (developing)

What changed: the new Democratic-majority Congress is now actively drafting competing AI safety bills, while the Trump administration's December 2025 Executive Order 14365 — which directed the DOJ to challenge state-level AI laws — creates a structural conflict with the states [14]. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act, which would create an Office of AI Safety and require independent validation of frontier models before release, remains the most viable federal vehicle, but Rep. Lori Trahan is reworking it so federal standards function as a floor, not a ceiling, explicitly allowing states to go further [15]. Democrats also introduced the SAFE AI Act, emphasising independent testing and an enforcement regime [15]. California is coordinating a seven-state coalition (New York, Massachusetts, Washington, Illinois, Colorado, Oregon) developing shared AI oversight standards due for preliminary publication in Q1 2027, which would create a de facto regulatory layer regardless of what the federal government does or does not pass [16]. For builders: California's seven-state coalition standards are due for preliminary publication in Q1 2027 [16] — the most concrete near-term compliance target while federal legislation remains unresolved.
